canonical_topic: Classification of coal by rank: lignite, sub-bituminous, bituminous, anthracite
definition: Coal used as fuel is classified into four main ranks by carbon content and heat energy — lignite, sub-bituminous, bituminous, and anthracite — with higher-carbon ranks generally containing more heat energy but being harder to ignite; other very high-carbon forms such as graphite and diamonds are technically coal but are not usable as fuel.
core_idea: There is a fundamental trade-off in coal fuel quality: as carbon content and heat energy rise from lignite to anthracite (and theoretically to graphite/diamond), ease of ignition falls, so extremely high-quality carbon forms become impractical to burn.
key_points: Coal is classified for fuel purposes mainly by carbon content and heat energy output.
The four fuel-grade coal types, in ascending order of carbon/energy content, are lignite, sub-bituminous, bituminous, and anthracite.
Graphite and diamond are nearly 100% carbon and technically coal, but are not practical fuels because they are hard to ignite.
Low-quality coal ignites easily but has lower energy content; higher-quality coal is harder to ignite but has substantially more energy content.
Extremely high-quality coal (e.g., graphite/diamond) has very high potential heat energy but is nearly impossible to ignite under normal conditions.
Coal types also vary in the type and amount of pollution they produce.
relationships: Ignition ease is inversely related to carbon content/energy density across the coal ranks.
trading_implications: Different coal grades are not interchangeable fuels; heat content and pollution profile differences affect delivered value and regulatory cost, so contracts should specify grade.
caveats: Higher carbon content does not automatically make a substance a usable fuel coal — ignitability matters as much as energy content (graphite/diamond illustrate this limit).
